scenario: Today's embodied AI track is about where robot data comes from and how to get more out of it. CIMI and TacClaw-Infinity both collect data without a robot. CIMI records where the fingers touch the object during human demonstrations, and TacClaw-Infinity gathers demonstrations in many real settings with a handheld gripper that senses touch. After deployment, two papers let robots keep learning from their own runs. One has a whole fleet share experience using only success or failure labels, and I3L lets an operator step in only when the policy goes wrong. Another group looks at how actions are represented. Vela writes a stretch of motion as a curve, and DiffWBC turns a humanoid controller into a diffusion model so it can be steered online. A large real-robot study also warns that offline metrics are a poor substitute for hardware tests.

papers.title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
papers.authors: Zhixuan Xu, Yichen Li, Bingchen Wu, Rui Wang, Yiwen Hou, Zixuan Liu, Tianyu Qiu, Lin Shao
papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.
papers.summary: Teaching a robot hand from human demonstrations is hard because human and robot hands have different shapes. If the conversion only tries to make the robot hand look like the human hand, the robot's fingertips often touch the object in different places than the human did, and grasps and pushes fail. CIMI puts contact first. During demonstrations it records the contact surfaces between fingers and object plus fingertip camera views; when converting to robot motion it aligns the contact points first and the finger pose second. The learned policy likewise predicts how the contact surface should move next, and a controller coordinates wrist and fingers to match it. Across six hand-task pairs on the LEAP and Wuji hands, mean full-task success beats baseline policies by at least 50 percentage points. ==When transferring human skills, matching contact matters more than matching hand shape==.

papers.title: LeRobot:  An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
papers.authors: Remi Cadene, Simon Alibert, Francesco Capuano, Michel Aractingi, Adil Zouitine, Pepijn Kooijmans, Jade Choghari, Martino Russi, Caroline Pascal, Steven Palma, Dana Aubakirova, Mustafa Shukor, Jess Moss, Alexander Soare, Quentin Lhoest, Quentin Gallouédec, Thomas Wolf
papers.abstract:
Robotics is undergoing a significant transformation powered by advances in high-level control techniques based on machine learning, giving rise to the field of robot learning.
Recent progress in robot learning has been accelerated by the increasing availability of affordable teleoperation systems, large-scale openly available datasets, and scalable learning-based methods.
However, development in the field of robot learning is often slowed by fragmented, closed-source tools designed to only address specific sub-components within the robotics stack.
In this paper, we present lerobot, an open-source library that integrates across the entire robotics stack, from low-level middleware communication for motor controls to large-scale dataset collection, storage and streaming.
The library is designed with a strong focus on real-world robotics, supporting accessible hardware platforms while remaining extensible to new embodiments.
It also supports efficient implementations for various state-of-the-art robot learning algorithms from multiple prominent paradigms, as well as a generalized asynchronous inference stack.
Unlike traditional pipelines which heavily rely on hand-crafted techniques, lerobot emphasizes scalable learning approaches that improve directly with more data and compute.
Designed for accessibility, scalability, and openness, lerobot lowers the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners to robotics while providing a platform for reproducible, state-of-the-art robot learning.
papers.summary: The robot learning toolchain is fragmented: motor communication, data collection, dataset formats, training algorithms and deployment each tend to use their own stack, so switching robots or datasets means re-assembling everything, and other people's results are hard to reproduce. LeRobot puts the whole chain into one open-source library: low-level motor control and support for low-cost hardware, a unified dataset format with streaming, implementations of several mainstream policy algorithms, and asynchronous inference. Its value is not a new algorithm but letting data and results from different labs be compared and reused within one set of tools.

papers.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
papers.summary: A low validation loss does not mean an imitation-learning policy works on the real robot. The authors had a five-fingered robot hand grasp and insert an RJ45 network connector and tested 281 policies on hardware to find which design choices actually decide success. The answer: how observations and actions are represented matters far more than the optimizer or sampling scheme. For point-cloud policies, keeping only the region around the target and expressing the points in the robot-base frame each raised success by 70 to 100 percentage points. Among dozens of offline metrics, only a few measuring whether predicted motion is smooth and direct correlated clearly with insertion success, and only within a single policy family. ==Offline metrics cannot yet replace real-robot testing==.

papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: Collective Experience Learning Across 96 Robots
papers.authors: Chao Yu, Shu'ang Yu, Hao Lin, Hongzhi Zang, Yuxiang Yan, Chenxi Jiang, Zhen Guo, Chuankang Li, Yihao Chen, Xin Xu, Xu Fu, Jiakai Zhou, Liangzhi Shi, Hongyi Ren, Yiwei Liu, Jing Wu, Yuanqing Wang, Chen Wu, Bo Dai, Chunyu Yang, Hongliang Huang, Shuoyu Yue, Weiqi Yin, Yinuo Chen, Ruihua Chen, Chunyang Zhu, Han Xiao, Yanghao Li, Ruipu Wu, Zhikai Cai, Xiu Chen, Xu Tan, Si Liu, Yuchen Yan, Jialin Zhang, Wen Zeng, Yiming Zhou, Zixiao Huang, Xinlei Chen, Guanghui Ren, Quanlu Zhang, Boxun Li, Maoqing Yao, Yu Wang
papers.abstract: Robot deployment generates experience that can support policy improvement, but continued reliance on expert corrective actions makes learning difficult to scale across growing fleets. We propose learning from fleet experience: using deployed robots' own executions as a source of supervision for further policy improvement. We call this paradigm Collective Experience Learning (CEL), in which robots pool execution experience to update a shared policy that returns to the fleet. Following expert-supervised initialization, we realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT). FERT uses failure contexts to retrieve relevant segments from successful trajectories and prioritizes their recorded actions for supervised updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. Operators provide binary episode-outcome labels and environment resets. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization despite local interruptions. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and generally improve performance across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raises success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support CEL as a scalable approach to improving robot policy reliability through experience generated during deployment.
papers.summary: Deployed robots work every day, but improving their policy usually still requires experts to demonstrate or correct actions, which scales poorly as fleets grow. This paper lets a fleet learn from its own execution records: operators only label each episode as success or failure and reset the scene. During training, the context of each failure is used to retrieve similar segments from successful trajectories, whose recorded actions are prioritized for imitation, and the updated shared policy is sent back to every robot. With collection time per robot held fixed, more robots generally means better results; on multi-stage phone packaging, learning across 96 robots raised success from 79.2% to 98.3%. ==Without extra expert demonstrations, success-or-failure labels alone can keep a whole fleet improving==.

papers.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
papers.authors: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang, Stef Ren, Jianwen Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, Ruohan Zhang
papers.abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.
papers.summary: Mobile manipulation policies trained on offline demonstrations tend to fail as soon as they meet situations not seen in training, and for long tasks where arm, torso and base must move together, recording more demonstrations cannot cover everything. I3L lets an operator take over when the robot goes wrong. The operator has a pair of leader arms that move in sync with the robot's arms, plus a pair of handheld controllers. Gripping a leader arm or pushing a controller hands full control to the person, who corrects the arms with the leader arms and steers torso and base with the controllers. The corrections are used for retraining, the new policy goes back on the robot, and the next round targets its new mistakes. After four rounds, autonomous success is on average 68.3 percentage points above the initial policy. With the same number of training trajectories it beats demonstration-only training by 35.6 points. ==Spending the demonstration budget where the policy actually fails beats recording more evenly==.

papers.title: DiffWBC: Unlocking Steerable General Humanoid Motion Tracking via One-Step Diffusion Whole-Body Control
papers.authors: Yifei Huang, Yazhao Yang, Weijia Li, Zhiheng Ma, Dian Shen
papers.abstract: General humanoid motion trackers typically rely on deterministic policies that cannot adapt online without brittle reference editing or costly retraining. We present DiffWBC, shifting whole-body control to a generative paradigm via a one-step diffusion model. By modeling distributions over future trajectories, DiffWBC unifies general tracking, test-time steering, and simulation-free failure discovery within a single controller: (1) Generative general tracking: DiffWBC requires a single forward pass per 50 Hz control step and can be distilled from an RL teacher or trained from scratch via model-based RL, achieving the lowest local tracking error among six general trackers on held-out benchmarks (20.1 mm on BONES) and deploying on a physical Unitree G1. (2) Zero-shot test-time steering: differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks modulate the frozen controller online, substantially outperforming kinematic reference editing (0.84 clean pass at 1.25 m ceiling vs. 0.10) and zero-shot generalizing across hurdles, spatial reaching, actuator faults, and tray balancing. (3) Simulation-free failure discovery: plan dispersion across generation noise effectively identifies physical tracking failures (91% precision in top 2%) without physics simulations; targeted fine-tuning on flagged clips resolves 50% of failure cases. Videos and interactive demonstrations are available at https://diffwbc.github.io/#selfassess.
papers.summary: Whole-body motion trackers for humanoids usually map a reference motion to a single set of joint commands, so making them dodge an obstacle means hand-editing the reference or retraining. DiffWBC turns the controller into a one-step diffusion model: it outputs a distribution over future trajectories while still needing only one forward pass per control step. The motion can then be steered online without changing any weights. Write a cost, such as how close the body gets to an obstacle, take its gradient with respect to the generator's input noise, and adjust the noise directly so the generated motion avoids the obstacle. When the robot must duck under a bar 1.25 m high, the share of runs that pass without touching the bar is 0.84, versus 0.10 for editing the reference motion. Sampling the same motion several times, the more the results spread, the more likely tracking will fail, which flags problem clips without physics simulation.

papers.title: RTPolicy: Real-Time (32.9 Hz) Multi-View Visuomotor Policy for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.authors: Xianbao Hou, Zehao Ni, Yonghao He, Lingfeng Qian, Xin Shi, Hu Su, Wei Sui, Cong Yang
papers.abstract: Low inference latency is critical for closed-loop robotic manipulation, especially under asynchronous inference, where action chunks must be updated promptly to correct accumulated deviations. However, existing visuomotor policies rely on computationally expensive visual backbones, resulting in high inference latency and deployment overhead. In this paper, we propose RTPolicy, a multi-view visuomotor policy that attains accurate manipulation with high inference efficiency. Its core design combines view-aware feature fusion with visual compression to aggregate complementary information across camera views into a compact token representation. The representation conditions a flow-matching action generator with the robot state and flow time, reducing the cost of action generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this design reduces the computational cost of visual representation and action generation while preserving visual information required for manipulation. On the RoboTwin~2.0 single-task clean evaluation across 50 tasks, RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 52.26\%, outperforming the strongest leaderboard baseline $π_0$ (46.4\%). We further evaluate RTPolicy under asynchronous streaming inference on a real bimanual platform, where RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 72.0\% and sustains real-time inference at 30.35 ms (32.9 Hz) on the RDK S600 and 149.72 ms (6.7 Hz) on the RDK S100, both in INT16. Project Page: https://d-robotics-ai-lab.github.io/RTPolicy.project.
papers.summary: When a robot runs inference while it moves, the slower the model, the later a drifting action gets corrected, and current visuomotor policies mostly depend on heavy visual backbones that are hard to run fast on edge chips. RTPolicy lets the camera views attend to each other through one cross-view attention layer. It then pools each view down to 4 tokens for a flow-matching action generator, cutting the compute for both visual encoding and action generation. On the RoboTwin simulation benchmark it reaches a mean success rate of 52.26%, the highest among the compared methods. On a real bimanual platform, one inference takes only 30.35 ms on the RDK S600 edge chip. ==Real-time on the edge need not cost accuracy if the multi-view images are compressed first==

papers.title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Fucai Zhu, Xidong Zhang, Yichi Zhang, Yipan Wang, Fubo Wang, Zibin Wu, Kaiqi Li, Jianhao Jiao, Shihan Lu, Di Hu, Mengdi Xu, Siyu Zhu, Xiaoxiao Long, Yao Yao, Xun Cao, Zhuo Xu, Koichi Hashimoto, Qifeng Chen, Zhe Li, Jianfei Yang, Haofei Lu, Danica Kragic, Shuicheng Yan, Jianghua Duan, Michael Yu Wang, Weihao Yuan
papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
papers.summary: Many dexterous actions depend on touch, such as telling whether a bottle is held firmly while sorting, yet tactile robot data is hard to collect at scale. TacClaw-Infinity collects data with a handheld gripper whose fingertips carry tactile sensors: people use it directly at home, in labs, factories, shops and outdoors, while it records camera views, fingertip touch and gripper trajectories, with no robot present. The result is over 10,000 hours of demonstrations covering more than a thousand task types, with uniform quality control, filtering and segment annotation. On three robots with different designs, adding tactile input raised the mean success rate of pi0.5 from 50.0% to 74.0%, with most of the gain on contact-dependent tasks such as bottle sorting.

papers.title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization
papers.authors: Yifan Li, Jiaxu Wang, Dongming Wu, Yicheng Jiang, Ryan Ji, Xiangyu Yue, Yanwei Fu
papers.abstract: Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce Vela, a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. Vela combines a compact spline-based action representation with motion-dependent temporal support and a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, allowing a fixed output budget to adapt its temporal resolution across motions. We pretrain Vela on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate it on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks, egg-cake cooking and potato shredding, obtaining promising results across simulation and physical manipulation. These results highlight the potential of continuous action representations as a foundation for future embodied foundation models.
papers.summary: Most of today's large robot models output a chunk of actions at a fixed rate, and neighbouring actions are nearly identical, so many output slots are wasted. Looking further ahead means giving up the local precision that contact requires. Vela instead outputs a fixed number of control points, each a position in action space, which together define a smooth spline that can be queried at any time. The model also outputs how far into the future this curve reaches. In training, that label is the longest span the fixed control points can represent within an error tolerance. So the curve reaches far when motion is smooth and stays short when contact needs precision, so the same control points are packed more densely. On a real long-horizon egg-cake cooking task, Vela's mean success across four subtasks is 67.5%, versus 37.5% for pi0.5. ==Switching from pointwise actions to curves lets the output budget go where it is needed==

papers.title: Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos
papers.abstract: Physical AI developers working with world models face two distinct challenges: adapting models to their sensors, tasks, and data, and getting those models into...
papers.summary: Using world models to simulate robots or autonomous driving runs into two hurdles: adapting the model to your own sensors and data, and deploying it reliably in applications. This NVIDIA technical blog introduces two Cosmos toolsets. Cosmos Framework provides modular pipelines for training, reinforcement learning, distillation, quantization and inference. Its newly released Nano simulation models generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR data for driving, bimanual robot and surgical scenes. The streaming variants take a policy's actions and generate the next frame in real time for closed-loop evaluation. Cosmos NIM packages these models as inference containers, with speculative decoding and other techniques giving average speedups of roughly 2 to 3 times. For teams that want to evaluate policies in generative simulation, the barrier to entry is clearly lower.
